content: Invoices and late payment interest What makes an invoice proper, when the government’s payment is due and how Prompt Payment Act interest is worked out when it is late. field  The government is required by law to pay its bills on time, and to pay interest when it does not. That law is the Prompt Payment Act. It only helps you if your invoice is correct and you know which dates start the clock. This guide covers both, with a worked interest calculation. The rule in one paragraph Under the Prompt Payment Act, an agency generally has to pay within 30 days of receiving a proper invoice or of accepting the work, whichever is later. If it pays after that, it owes interest f

title: The rule in one paragraph
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Under the Prompt Payment Act, an agency generally has to pay within 30 days of receiving a proper invoice or of accepting the work, whichever is later. If it pa...
content: The rule in one paragraph Invoices and late payment interest Under the Prompt Payment Act, an agency generally has to pay within 30 days of receiving a proper invoice or of accepting the work, whichever is later. If it pays after that, it owes interest for every day it is late, at a rate the Treasury sets twice a year. The interest is owed automatically. You should not have to ask for it. The details are in the contract. Look for the prompt payment clause, long numbered FAR 52.232-25, and for any payment terms particular to your contract in Sections G and I.

title: What makes an invoice proper
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: The clock does not start on an invoice that is missing something. A proper invoice includes: 1. your company’s name and address 2. the invoice date and an invoi...
content: What makes an invoice proper Invoices and late payment interest The clock does not start on an invoice that is missing something. A proper invoice includes: 1. your company’s name and address 2. the invoice date and an invoice number 3. the contract number, and the order number and line item number where they apply 4. a description of what was delivered, with quantity, unit of measure, unit price and extended price 5. shipping and payment terms 6. the name and address where payment is to be sent 7. the name, title and phone number of a person to contact about the invoice 8. your taxpayer identification number and electronic payment details, when the contract requires them on the invoice 9. anything else the contract asks for The contract can add to this list. Read the invoicing instructions before you send the first one, and build a template that matches.

title: If the invoice is rejected
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: When an invoice is not proper, the agency is supposed to send it back within 7 days of receiving it and say what is wrong. Fix it and send it again. The 30 days...
content: If the invoice is rejected Invoices and late payment interest When an invoice is not proper, the agency is supposed to send it back within 7 days of receiving it and say what is wrong. Fix it and send it again. The 30 days are counted from the corrected invoice. If the agency takes longer than 7 days to tell you, the extra days are taken off the time it has to pay.

title: Find the due date
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Three dates decide when payment is due. Write each one down as it happens. | Date | What it is | | --- | --- | | Invoice received | The day the billing office n...
content: Find the due date Invoices and late payment interest Three dates decide when payment is due. Write each one down as it happens. | Date | What it is | | --- | --- | | Invoice received | The day the billing office named in the contract receives your proper invoice | | Acceptance | The day the government accepts the goods or services | | Due date | 30 days after the later of the two, unless the contract sets a different period | Two details catch people out: - Acceptance can be deemed. For the purpose of counting interest, acceptance is treated as happening on the 7th day after delivery if the government has not actually accepted or rejected the work by then, unless the contract sets a different period. An agency cannot hold the clock by leaving a delivery unreviewed. - The payment date is the date of the transfer , not the day the money shows in your account. Contracts can set shorter periods, and some categories of goods have their own by law. The contract is where to look.

title: The interest rate
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: The Treasury sets the rate for each half of the year, starting January 1 and July 1, and publishes it on its Prompt Payment pages and in the Federal Register. F...
content: The interest rate Invoices and late payment interest The Treasury sets the rate for each half of the year, starting January 1 and July 1, and publishes it on its Prompt Payment pages and in the Federal Register. For July 1 to December 31, 2026 the rate is 4.75 percent a year. The rate that applies to a late payment is the one in effect on the day after the due date. It stays the same for that payment even if a new rate is published while you are waiting. The rate changes every six months. Before you rely on any figure, including the one above or one built into a tool, compare it with the Treasury’s published table for the period your due date falls in.

title: Work out the interest
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: For a payment up to 30 days late, interest is simple interest on a 360-day year: Days late run from the day after the due date through the day payment is made. ...
content: Work out the interest Invoices and late payment interest For a payment up to 30 days late, interest is simple interest on a 360-day year: Days late run from the day after the due date through the day payment is made. A made-up example: an invoice for $20,000.00 was due on September 1 and paid on September 21. That is 20 days late, at 4.75 percent. When a payment is more than 30 days late, the interest that has built up is added to the amount owed at the end of each 30-day period, and the next period’s interest is worked out on the larger figure. Take the same invoice paid 45 days late: | Period | Owed at start | Days | Interest | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | First 30 days | $20,000.00 | 30 | $79.17 | | Next 15 days | $20,079.17 | 15 | $39.74 | | Total | | 45 | $118.91 |

title: The limits
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: - Under one dollar. An interest amount of less than $1.00 is not paid. - One year. Interest stops building after a year. It also stops if you file a formal clai...
content: The limits Invoices and late payment interest - Under one dollar. An interest amount of less than $1.00 is not paid. - One year. Interest stops building after a year. It also stops if you file a formal claim under the contract’s disputes process, where different interest rules take over. - Disputes. No interest runs while there is a real disagreement about the amount owed or whether the work meets the contract. - Financing payments. Progress payments and other contract financing are not covered. The Act applies to payments for delivered and accepted work. - Your own delay. Interest does not run for time lost to a defective invoice the agency flagged on time.

title: If the interest is not paid
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Interest should arrive with the late payment, without a request. If it does not, there is a further penalty, and this one you do have to ask for. - The agency p...
content: If the interest is not paid Invoices and late payment interest Interest should arrive with the late payment, without a request. If it does not, there is a further penalty, and this one you do have to ask for. - The agency paid late and did not include the interest. - It still has not paid the interest 10 days after the payment. - You send a written demand to the payment office no later than 40 days after the payment was made. The additional penalty is equal to the unpaid interest, with a minimum of $25 and a maximum of $5,000. The 40-day limit is strict, which is one more reason to keep the dates.

title: Sending invoices to the Department of Defense
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Defense contracts normally require invoices to be submitted electronically through Wide Area WorkFlow, which is part of the department’s Procurement Integrated ...
content: Sending invoices to the Department of Defense Invoices and late payment interest Defense contracts normally require invoices to be submitted electronically through Wide Area WorkFlow, which is part of the department’s Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment at piee.eb.mil. You register your company there, and your contract tells you which document type to submit and the codes that route it to the right offices. A document rejected in that system is the same as a rejected invoice. Check its status, do not assume.

title: What the Act does not cover
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: - Payments from a prime contractor to a subcontractor. The Act governs what the government pays its own contractors. What a prime owes you is set by your subcon...
content: What the Act does not cover Invoices and late payment interest - Payments from a prime contractor to a subcontractor. The Act governs what the government pays its own contractors. What a prime owes you is set by your subcontract. Negotiate the payment terms before you sign. - Other transaction agreements and grants. These have their own terms. - Amounts withheld under the contract , such as retainage, until the condition for release is met. Small business primes and subcontractors may benefit from accelerated payment policies, under which agencies try to pay sooner than the law requires. That is a goal agencies work toward. It does not change the date from which interest runs.

title: Keep the record
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: For each invoice, keep a line with: - delivery date - acceptance date, or the date acceptance was deemed - date the invoice was received by the billing office -...
content: Keep the record Invoices and late payment interest For each invoice, keep a line with: - delivery date - acceptance date, or the date acceptance was deemed - date the invoice was received by the billing office - due date - payment date and amount - interest owed, and interest received With those six facts you can check any interest figure by hand, and you can show the payment office exactly where a number comes from.

content: What every tool will have in common Getting started When tools ship, each must satisfy five mandatory listing criteria: 1. Public sources only: Built exclusively from official government regulations, standards, and published guidance. 5. Clear operational limits: Explicit statements about what the tool does not cover, reminding users that output is not professional advice.

title: Buying and contracts
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Acquisition. The government’s word for buying: the whole process from deciding a need to closing out the contract. - Amendment. A written change to a solicita...
content: Buying and contracts Glossary - Acquisition. The government’s word for buying: the whole process from deciding a need to closing out the contract. - Amendment. A written change to a solicitation before award. Each one is part of the solicitation. - Award. The government’s decision to give a contract to an offeror, and the act of signing it. - BPA (blanket purchase agreement). A standing arrangement for repeated small purchases from the same vendor. - CFR (Code of Federal Regulations). The collected regulations of federal agencies, arranged in numbered titles. Title 48 holds the acquisition regulations. - CLIN (contract line item number). A numbered line in a contract for one thing being bought, with its quantity and price. A SLIN is a sub-line under it. - Contracting officer (CO or KO). The government official with authority to sign, change and end a contract. Only a contracting officer can commit the government. - COR (contracting officer’s representative). A government employee who monitors the work day to day. A COR cannot change the contract. - DFARS (Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement). The Department of Defense’s additions to the FAR. - FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation). The main rulebook for how federal executive agencies buy goods and services. - GWAC (government-wide acquisition contract). A large ordering contract for technology that any agency can use. - IDIQ (indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity). A contract that sets terms and prices in advance and is then used by placing individual orders. - IFB (invitation for bids). A solicitation for sealed bids, awarded on price. - Modification. A written change to a contract after award. - Offeror. A company that submits a proposal. Also called a bidder, quoter or respondent, depending on the kind of solicitation. - Option. A right the government holds to extend a contract or buy more at prices already agreed. - OT (other transaction). An agreement that is not a FAR contract, used by some agencies for research and prototypes. Also called an OTA. - Period of performance. The dates between which the work is done. - Prime contractor. The company that holds the contract with the government. A subcontractor holds a contract with the prime. - PWS (performance work statement). A description of the work in terms of results required. - RFI (request for information). Market research. Not a solicitation. - RFP (request for proposals). A solicitation for negotiated contracts. - RFQ (request for quotation). A request for prices, usually for simpler purchases. - SBIR and STTR. Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer: programs that fund research by small businesses in phases. - Section L and Section M. The parts of a solicitation that give proposal instructions (Section L) and evaluation factors for award (Section M). - Section M. The evaluation factors for award in a federal solicitation, used metaphorically on this site for the Prior Art decision engine. - Solicitation. The government’s written request for offers. - SOO (statement of objectives). A short statement of goals. The offeror proposes how to meet them. - Sources sought. A notice asking who is capable of doing a piece of work. Market research, like an RFI. - SOW (statement of work). A description of the work to be done. - Task order. An individual order for services placed under an ordering contract. - UCF (uniform contract format). The traditional layout of a solicitation in lettered Sections A through M.

title: Contract types and evaluation
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Best value tradeoff. A basis for award in which the government may pay more for a better proposal. - Cost reimbursement. A contract type in which the governme...
content: Contract types and evaluation Glossary - Best value tradeoff. A basis for award in which the government may pay more for a better proposal. - Cost reimbursement. A contract type in which the government pays the contractor’s allowable costs, usually plus a fee. CPFF, cost plus fixed fee, is the common form. - CPARS (Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System). Where the government records how a contractor performed. Other agencies read it when judging past performance. - FFP (firm fixed price). A contract type with a set price that does not change with the contractor’s costs. - LPTA (lowest price technically acceptable). A basis for award in which the lowest-priced proposal that meets the requirements wins. - Past performance. How well a company did on earlier, similar work. A common evaluation factor. - T&M (time and materials). A contract type that pays fixed hourly rates for labor, plus materials at cost. Labor hour, LH, is the same without materials.

title: Pricing and cost accounting
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Allocable. Able to be assigned to a contract because it benefits that contract or the business as a whole. - Allocation base. The measure an indirect cost poo...
content: Pricing and cost accounting Glossary - Allocable. Able to be assigned to a contract because it benefits that contract or the business as a whole. - Allocation base. The measure an indirect cost pool is divided by to make a rate, such as direct labor dollars. - Allowable cost. A cost the government will pay on a cost-based contract: reasonable, allocable, consistent with accounting standards and the contract, and not excluded by FAR Part 31. - CAS (Cost Accounting Standards). Accounting rules for large negotiated contracts. Small businesses are exempt. - Certified cost or pricing data. Detailed cost information a contractor must certify as accurate on large negotiated awards without adequate competition. The dollar threshold is set by law and differs between defense and civilian agencies. - Cost pool. A group of indirect costs gathered together to be shared out. - DCAA (Defense Contract Audit Agency). The agency that audits contractors’ costs and accounting systems for the Department of Defense. - DCMA (Defense Contract Management Agency). The agency that administers defense contracts after award. - Direct cost. A cost incurred for one specific contract. - Escalation. A planned yearly increase in a rate or price. - Fee. Profit on a cost-based contract. - Fringe. The cost of employee benefits and payroll taxes, usually expressed as a rate on labor. - Fully burdened rate. An hourly rate that includes the wage, all indirect costs and fee. - G&A (general and administrative). The cost of running the company as a whole. - Incurred cost submission. The yearly report of actual indirect costs that a contractor with cost-reimbursement work sends to the government. - Indirect cost. A cost that supports more than one contract or the business generally. - ODC (other direct cost). A direct cost that is not labor, such as travel or materials. - Overhead. The cost of supporting the people who do contract work. - Proper invoice. An invoice with every element the contract and the prompt payment rules require. - Prompt Payment Act. The law that sets when agencies must pay and requires interest when they pay late. - Provisional billing rate. An indirect rate used for invoicing during the year, settled against actual costs afterward. - Unallowable cost. A cost the government will not pay, such as entertainment or alcohol. - Wage determination. A list of minimum wages and benefits for job classes on certain service and construction contracts. - WAWF (Wide Area WorkFlow). The Department of Defense’s system for submitting invoices and receiving reports. - Wrap rate. The multiplier that turns a wage into a burdened rate.

title: Security and compliance
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Affirmation. A statement by a senior company official that the company meets, and will keep meeting, its security requirements. - ATO (authorization to operat...
content: Security and compliance Glossary - Affirmation. A statement by a senior company official that the company meets, and will keep meeting, its security requirements. - ATO (authorization to operate). A government official’s formal decision that a system may be used. - Banner marking. The marking at the top of each page of a document containing CUI. - C3PAO. A third-party organization accredited to carry out CMMC assessments. - CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification). The Department of Defense program for verifying that contractors protect FCI and CUI. - CDI (covered defense information). The term in the DFARS for CUI handled under a defense contract. - CUI (controlled unclassified information). Unclassified information that a law, regulation or government-wide policy requires to be protected. - CUI Registry. The official list of CUI categories, kept by the National Archives. - Designation indicator. The block on a CUI document that names who controls it. - Export controls. Rules limiting who may receive certain technical data and items. The ITAR covers defense articles and the EAR covers dual-use items. - FCI (federal contract information). Non-public information provided by or created for the government under a contract. - FedRAMP. The government’s program for authorizing cloud services. - NIST. The National Institute of Standards and Technology, which publishes the security standards most contracts refer to. - NIST SP 800-53. The catalog of security and privacy controls for federal systems. - NIST SP 800-171. The requirements for protecting CUI on non-federal systems. - NIST SP 800-172. Enhanced requirements for CUI at higher risk. - POA&M (plan of action and milestones). The list of unmet requirements, with a plan and a date for each. - RMF (Risk Management Framework). The process federal agencies use to authorize their own systems. - SPRS (Supplier Performance Risk System). The Department of Defense system where assessment scores and affirmations are recorded. - SSP (system security plan). The document describing a system and how it meets each security requirement.

title: Technical formats and disconnected work
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Air gap. A physical separation between a network and all others. - CA (certificate authority). An organization that issues and signs certificates. - Certifica...
content: Technical formats and disconnected work Glossary - Air gap. A physical separation between a network and all others. - CA (certificate authority). An organization that issues and signs certificates. - Certificate chain. The sequence from a server’s certificate through intermediates to a trusted root. - Checksum. A short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents. Also called a hash. - Client-side. Running on the user’s own computer, in the browser, and not on a server. - CSP (content security policy). An instruction from a web page telling the browser what it may load and where it may connect. - Digest. The checksum that identifies a container image by its contents. - Lockfile. A file recording the exact version and checksum of every dependency of a project. - Manifest. A list describing the contents of a package, an image or a transfer. - OSCAL (Open Security Controls Assessment Language). NIST’s formats for security controls, plans and assessment results as structured data. - SBOM (software bill of materials). A list of the components a piece of software is built from. - SHA-256. The checksum algorithm in general use for verifying files. - SRG (Security Requirements Guide). Security requirements for a class of technology. A STIG applies one to a specific product. - STIG (Security Technical Implementation Guide). Configuration rules for a specific product, published by DISA. - X.509. The standard format for certificates. - XCCDF. The XML format STIGs are published in.

title: Registration, codes and small business
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - 8(a). A Small Business Administration business development program for small businesses owned by disadvantaged individuals. - Affiliation. A relationship of c...
content: Registration, codes and small business Glossary - 8(a). A Small Business Administration business development program for small businesses owned by disadvantaged individuals. - Affiliation. A relationship of control between businesses that causes their sizes to be added together. - CAGE code. A five-character code identifying a business location. - HUBZone. Historically Underutilized Business Zone: an area, and the program for small businesses located in one. - Limitations on subcontracting. The rule limiting how much of a set-aside contract a small prime can pass to others. - Micro-purchase threshold. The dollar value under which purchases can be made without competition. - NAICS (North American Industry Classification System). Six-digit codes classifying businesses by industry. Each has a size standard. - NDC (nontraditional defense contractor). A business that has not recently performed defense work subject to full Cost Accounting Standards coverage. - PSC (product and service code). A four-character code describing what is being bought. - Rule of two. The rule that a purchase is set aside when two capable small businesses can be expected to offer at fair prices. - SAM (System for Award Management). The government’s register of the businesses it contracts with, and its site for posting opportunities. - SBA. The Small Business Administration. - SDVOSB. Service-disabled veteran-owned small business. - Set-aside. A competition limited to small businesses, or to one program’s participants. - Simplified acquisition threshold. The dollar value under which simpler buying procedures apply. - Size standard. The largest a business can be, in receipts or employees, and still count as small for a NAICS code. - Sole source. An award made without competition. - UEI (Unique Entity ID). The twelve-character identifier assigned to a business in SAM. - WOSB and EDWOSB. Women-owned small business, and economically disadvantaged women-owned small business.

content: Agencies and names Glossary - DISA. The Defense Information Systems Agency. It publishes the STIGs. - DoD. The Department of Defense. Since 2025 the department has also used the name Department of War on its own sites and correspondence. The regulations and contract clauses cited in these guides still say Department of Defense, and so do the guides. - GSA. The General Services Administration. It runs SAM.gov and many government-wide contracts. - NARA. The National Archives and Records Administration. It oversees the CUI program across the government. - OMB. The Office of Management and Budget. - Treasury. The Department of the Treasury. Its Bureau of the Fiscal Service publishes the Prompt Payment interest rate.

content: Project and authoring Glossary - Antigravity. An agentic AI coding assistant used during development to draft code, tests, and documentation under human direction. - Claude Code. An agentic AI coding tool used during development to draft code, tests, and documentation under human direction. - Clean room. Building software from functional specifications and public regulations without examining or copying another tool's proprietary code, text, or design. - Decision log. A public record documenting every evaluation outcome, score rationale, drafting agent, and maintainer decision. - Knockout gate. title: Labor rates and wrap rates
subtitle: Guide · Section FIELD
summary: How a wage becomes a billing rate: direct and indirect costs, fringe, overhead, G&A and fee, with a worked example you can check by hand.
content: Labor rates and wrap rates How a wage becomes a billing rate: direct and indirect costs, fringe, overhead, G&A and fee, with a worked example you can check by hand. field  When the government buys labor, the hourly price has to cover far more than the wage. It carries a share of payroll taxes, benefits, rent, software, accounting and every other cost of running the company, plus profit. This guide explains how that price is built, using one made-up company from start to finish. Every number in it is invented. Direct and indirect costs Every cost a company has falls on one side of a line. - A direct cost is spent for one specific contract. The hours an engineer wor

title: Direct and indirect costs
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Every cost a company has falls on one side of a line. - A direct cost is spent for one specific contract. The hours an engineer works on that contract, a server...
content: Direct and indirect costs Labor rates and wrap rates Every cost a company has falls on one side of a line. - A direct cost is spent for one specific contract. The hours an engineer works on that contract, a server bought for it, a trip taken for it. - An indirect cost supports the business as a whole or more than one contract. Rent, the accounting system, the time spent writing proposals, health insurance. Direct costs are charged to the contract they belong to. Indirect costs are gathered into groups called pools , and each pool is shared out across contracts in proportion to some measure of activity, called a base . The rule that matters is consistency. The same kind of cost, in the same circumstances, has to be treated the same way every time. A cost cannot be direct on one contract and indirect on another because that is convenient.

title: The three usual pools
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: A small company commonly has three pools. The names are standard. What goes in each, and what each is divided by, is a choice the company makes and then sticks ...
content: The three usual pools Labor rates and wrap rates A small company commonly has three pools. The names are standard. What goes in each, and what each is divided by, is a choice the company makes and then sticks to. | Pool | What is usually in it | A common base | | --- | --- | --- | | Fringe | Payroll taxes, health insurance, retirement contributions, paid leave | Total labor dollars | | Overhead | Costs of supporting the people who do contract work: their supervisors’ time, tools, training, office space | Direct labor dollars, with or without fringe | | General and administrative (G&A) | Costs of running the company as a whole: executives, accounting, legal, insurance, proposal writing | All other costs | Larger companies split these further, for example into separate overhead pools for work done at their own offices and at government sites. A very small company may have only fringe and G&A.

title: Turn pools into rates
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: A rate is a pool divided by its base, over the company’s fiscal year. Take a made-up company with these annual figures: | Item | Amount | | --- | ---: | | Direc...
content: Turn pools into rates Labor rates and wrap rates A rate is a pool divided by its base, over the company’s fiscal year. Take a made-up company with these annual figures: | Item | Amount | | --- | ---: | | Direct labor: wages for hours worked on contracts | $600,000 | | Indirect labor: wages for everything else | $100,000 | | Fringe pool | $210,000 | | Overhead pool | $156,000 | | G&A pool | $112,320 | Fringe rate. The fringe pool is divided by all labor, direct and indirect: Overhead rate. This company applies overhead to direct labor plus the fringe on it: G&A rate. This company applies G&A to everything beneath it: The rates only mean something together with their bases. “Our overhead is 20 percent” is not comparable with another company’s 20 percent unless both are divided by the same thing.

subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates

content: Build the rate for one hour Labor rates and wrap rates Now price one hour of an engineer paid $60.00 an hour. Each layer is applied to the running total beneath it. | Step | Rate | Adds | Running total | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Hourly wage | | | $60.00 | | Fringe | 30% | $18.00 | $78.00 | | Overhead | 20% | $15.60 | $93.60 | | G&A | 12% | $11.23 | $104.83 | | Fee | 8% | $8.39 | $113.22 | The fully burdened rate is $113.22 an hour.

title: The wrap rate
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: The wrap rate is the single multiplier that takes you from the wage to the burdened rate. It is the layers multiplied together: So every dollar of wage costs th...
content: The wrap rate Labor rates and wrap rates The wrap rate is the single multiplier that takes you from the wage to the burdened rate. It is the layers multiplied together: So every dollar of wage costs this company about $1.75 to deliver, and is priced at about $1.89. Check: $60.00 × 1.8870 = $113.22. People quote wrap rates both with and without fee. When you compare yours with someone else’s, ask which.

title: Conventions that change the answer
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Two companies with identical costs can show different rates, because they made different structural choices. None of these is wrong. Each has to be applied cons...
content: Conventions that change the answer Labor rates and wrap rates Two companies with identical costs can show different rates, because they made different structural choices. None of these is wrong. Each has to be applied consistently. - What overhead is applied to. Direct labor alone, or direct labor plus fringe. Applying 20 percent to $60.00 gives a different result from applying it to $78.00. - What G&A is applied to. All costs beneath it, known as total cost input, or all costs except subcontracts and materials, known as a value-added base. The second gives a higher rate on a smaller base. - Where paid leave goes. In the fringe pool, or left in the labor base. - Whether fee is applied to everything. Some solicitations limit or forbid fee on travel, materials or subcontracts. Before you trust any calculator, including one listed here, find out which conventions it uses. Check a tool’s answer shows how to test that with one round-number example.

title: From a salary to an hourly wage
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Rates are applied to an hourly wage, so a salary has to be converted. A full-time year is 2,080 hours: 52 weeks of 40 hours. Nobody works all 2,080 hours on con...
content: From a salary to an hourly wage Labor rates and wrap rates Rates are applied to an hourly wage, so a salary has to be converted. A full-time year is 2,080 hours: 52 weeks of 40 hours. Nobody works all 2,080 hours on contracts. Holidays, leave and sick time come out. How you handle that is tied to the leave convention above: - If paid leave is in the fringe pool , divide the salary by 2,080 and let the fringe rate pay for the time off. - If paid leave is not in fringe , divide the salary by the hours actually worked, often somewhere around 1,880 to 1,920, which gives a higher hourly wage and a lower fringe rate. Doing both at once counts leave twice. Doing neither leaves it out.

title: Costs the government will not pay
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: On contracts priced or reimbursed on the basis of cost, a cost has to be allowable to be included. The cost principles are in FAR Part 31. A cost is allowable w...
content: Costs the government will not pay Labor rates and wrap rates On contracts priced or reimbursed on the basis of cost, a cost has to be allowable to be included. The cost principles are in FAR Part 31. A cost is allowable when it is reasonable, can properly be assigned to the contract, follows accepted accounting practice and the contract’s terms, and is not ruled out by a specific cost principle. Some costs are ruled out whatever the circumstances. They include: | Cost | Cost principle | | --- | --- | | Most advertising and public relations | FAR 31.205-1 | | Bad debts | FAR 31.205-3 | | Contributions and donations | FAR 31.205-8 | | Entertainment | FAR 31.205-14 | | Fines and penalties | FAR 31.205-15 | | Interest on borrowing | FAR 31.205-20 | | Lobbying | FAR 31.205-22 | | Alcoholic beverages | FAR 31.205-51 | Unallowable costs still exist and still have to be paid. They come out of profit instead of going into the rates. Your accounting system needs to keep them in separate accounts so they can be left out of every pool.

title: When these rules apply to you
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: How much of this the government looks at depends on the kind of contract. | Contract type | How the price is set | How closely costs are examined | | --- | --- ...
content: When these rules apply to you Labor rates and wrap rates How much of this the government looks at depends on the kind of contract. | Contract type | How the price is set | How closely costs are examined | | --- | --- | --- | | Fixed price, commercial or competed | You offer a price. The government compares offers | Usually not at all. Your rates are your own business | | Time and materials, labor hour | Fixed hourly rates by labor category, times hours worked | The rates are set at award. The hours are checked | | Cost reimbursement | The government pays your allowable costs plus a fee | Closely. Rates are billed provisionally, then settled each year against actual costs | Even on a fixed-price bid, building your rates properly tells you whether the price you are offering covers your costs. For cost-reimbursement work, a few more things follow. You bill during the year at provisional rates agreed in advance. After the year ends you submit your actual indirect costs, and the difference is settled. Your accounting system has to be able to produce those figures. The Defense Contract Audit Agency publishes a plain-language manual for small contractors on what that takes. The Cost Accounting Standards, a further set of rules for large contracts, do not apply to contracts with small businesses.

title: Lay out the price table
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Section B of a solicitation lists what is being bought as numbered line items. For labor, a line usually multiplies a rate by a quantity of hours: | Line item |...
content: Lay out the price table Labor rates and wrap rates Section B of a solicitation lists what is being bought as numbered line items. For labor, a line usually multiplies a rate by a quantity of hours: | Line item | Description | Quantity | Unit | Unit price | Amount | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | | 0001 | Senior engineer, base year | 1,880 | Hour | $113.22 | $212,853.60 | | 0002 | Travel, not to exceed | 1 | Lot | | $10,000.00 | | 1001 | Senior engineer, option year 1 | 1,880 | Hour | $116.62 | $219,245.60 | Things to settle before you fill one in: - Use the solicitation’s line items, labor categories and hours , not your own. If a pricing workbook is attached, that file is the deliverable. - Rounding. Round the hourly rate to the cent first and then multiply, unless told otherwise. Multiplying an unrounded rate gives a different total. - Option years. Wages rise. The example applies 3 percent to the base-year rate for the option year. State the escalation you used, and apply it the way the solicitation asks. - Wage floors. Some service contracts set minimum wages and benefits for certain job classes through a wage determination attached to the solicitation. Your base wage cannot be lower. - What carries fee. Check whether travel and other direct costs may include fee or G&A.

content: The contract structure How to navigate this site Federal solicitations under FAR Part 15 follow the Uniform Contract Format (UCF). The UCF organizes complex requirements into standardized lettered sections so that contractors always know where to find line items, statements of work, and submission instructions. ClearedStack borrows this exact structure across its pages. Instead of arbitrary marketing layouts, the site uses UCF conventions to label its data, navigation, and documentation: | UCF Section | Title in Federal Contracting | ClearedStack Location | What you find there | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Section B | Supplies or services and prices/costs | Home and Tools | The 5 Contract Line Item Number (CLIN) categories, all priced at a firm-fixed-price of $0.00. | | Section C | Description/specifications/statement of work | Home and Tools | The statement of work for all 18 single-purpose browser tools. | | Section F | Deliveries or performance | Home | The delivery roadmap across three phases: the free arsenal, the community, and the institution. | | Section H | Special contract requirements | Home and About | The four core ground rules: free, open source, client-side execution, and independent governance. | | Section L | Instructions, conditions and notices to offerors | Guides | The documentation library, numbered from L.1 through L.6 (Start here, Field guides, Hosting, Contributing, Reference, How this project is run). | | Section M | Evaluation factors for award | How we decide | The Prior Art decision engine (draft): ten stages, five knockout gates, scoring rubric, and public decision log. | Learning this layout once helps you navigate both ClearedStack and federal requests for proposals (RFPs). You can move between them at any time using the navigation links in the persistent header ( SiteHeader ) at the top of every page, or the index links in the footer ( SiteFooter ) at the bottom. The footer also carries our AI disclosure—stating that the site is built with Claude Code and Antigravity and reviewed by a person—linking to How AI is used to build this project. 1. Home ( / ) The home page provides an executive summary of the project: - Hero & Mission: A concise statement of why ClearedStack exists—to help small businesses and engineers get through contracting paperwork without buying enterprise software or hiring compliance consultants. - Section B Price Schedule: An interactive pricing table laying out the five tool categories as CLINs 0001 through 0005, showing unit prices and total evaluated price ($0.00). - Section C Catalog Preview: Summary cards for all five areas showing the tools planned under each CLIN. - Section H Principles: The mandatory operational boundaries (free forever, MIT licensed, strictly client-side, unaffiliated with the government). - Section F Roadmap: The phased delivery timeline showing current focus and future trajectory. 2. Tools ( /tools/ ) The tool catalog is the functional core of the site. It lists all 18 planned tools organized by their 4-digit CLINs. On this page, you can: - Filter tools in real time using the interactive search input. - Jump directly to specific categories using category anchor buttons ( pricing , proposal , cyber , market , devsecops ). - Check development statuses ( Planned , In development , Live ). - Access the direct links and open-source source code repositories as tools become live. 3. Guides ( /guides/ ) The documentation hub contains detailed operational guides. It is structured under UCF Section L ("Instructions to offerors"): - Metrics Bar: Summary counts of total guides, sections, combined reading time, and pricing ($0.00). - Curated Reading Routes: Tailored sequence paths designed for specific visitor objectives. - Section Index (L.1–L.6): An interactive, searchable library of all guides with real-time text matching and section jump anchors. - Short Answers: Quick answers to common questions regarding data security, costs, accounts, and trust. 4. How we decide ( /how-we-decide/ ) The decision engine under UCF Section M ("Evaluation factors for award"): - Prior Art Process (Draft): How existing tools are discovered, observed from public pages, screened, scored, and decided. - Five Knockout Gates: The non-negotiable checks every idea must pass before scoring. - Advisory Rubric: The 100-point rubric and public decision log with human owner accountability. 5. About ( /about/ ) The project background and governance statement: - The Problem & Mission: Why good engineers should not need a full compliance department to bid on federal work. - Architecture: Why each tool is built as an independent, auditable open-source repository rather than a monolithic platform. - Ground Rules: Absolute rules governing no revenue, zero telemetry or tracking, public sources only, and verifiable math. - Legal Disclaimer: Clear statements that ClearedStack is not a government agency, does not grant security clearances or CMMC certifications, and provides self-service reference tools rather than legal or accounting advice. - Contact: Direct links to the GitHub organization and maintainer email.

content: Finding tools in the catalog How to navigate this site All tools are indexed on the Tools page. The catalog is organized into five CLIN categories: | CLIN | Anchor Link | Area | Focus | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0001 | pricing | Pricing & cost accounting | Fully burdened wrap rates, indirect cost pools, Section B pricing tables, and Prompt Payment Act late interest. | | 0002 | proposal | Proposal & capture | RFP requirement shredding, compliance matrices, acronym tables, and page budget allocations. | | 0003 | cyber | Cybersecurity & compliance | NIST SP 800-171 / CMMC readiness checklists, CUI marking generators, DISA STIG reference lookups, and OSCAL validation. | | 0004 | market | Market research & small business | NAICS-to-PSC code crosswalks, Nontraditional Defense Contractor (NDC) eligibility, and small business set-aside guides. | | 0005 | devsecops | Tactical & DevSecOps | Offline container manifest inspectors, X.509 certificate chain decoders, and air-gap transfer checksum helpers. | Using the interactive search filter At the top of the catalog is an interactive search input: - Instant filtering: As you type, the tool list updates immediately without reloading the page. - Multi-field matching: The search scans across tool names (such as "Wrap Rate Calculator"), summaries (such as "cost pools"), and category titles simultaneously. - Multi-word AND logic: Typing labor rate finds tools containing both "labor" and "rate", filtering out irrelevant items. - Live tally: A counter to the right of the search input displays the exact count of matches ( X of 18 tools ), announced directly to assistive technologies. - Clearing your query: Press Escape , click the clear button ( ✕ ) inside the search box, or delete the search text to restore the complete catalog. Reading status labels Every tool card carries a color-coded status badge: - Planned: The tool is defined in the catalog and scheduled for implementation. Work has not yet begun. All 18 tools are currently marked Planned. - In development: The tool is actively being coded and tested in its dedicated repository. - Live: The tool is completed, tested, and operational. Its title links directly to the browser-based application, and a "Source" link points to its public repository. Signaling demand and prioritizing tools ClearedStack builds tools based on what users ask for first. If a planned tool would save you or your team hours of manual spreadsheet work, let the maintainers know. 3. Open a feature request issue on GitHub or send an email to contact@clearedstack.com. 4. Describe your specific use case, governing contract clauses, or input formats. User demand determines the active build sequence. content: Using the guides library How to navigate this site The Guides page contains in-depth documentation covering contracting regulations, site architecture, self-hosting, and contribution. The Section L organization Guides are grouped into six logical sections under UCF Section L: - L.1 Start here: Essential onboarding guides covering site navigation, browser data isolation, result verification, and core operating principles. - L.2 Field guides: Detailed primers on government contracting mechanics—reading RFPs, answering requirements, building labor rates, submitting proper invoices, protecting CUI, handling STIGs and OSCAL, and working on disconnected networks. - L.3 Host your own copy: Complete engineering guides for deploying ClearedStack on Docker, Kubernetes, bare static web servers, or air-gapped security enclaves. - L.4 Contribute: Step-by-step instructions for submitting tool requests, reporting regulatory errors, building compliant client-side tools, and maintaining this website. - L.5 Reference: Quick lookups including a comprehensive contracting acronym glossary, regulatory source links, and answers to common questions. - L.6 How this project is run: How ClearedStack discovers and observes existing tools, scores ideas in public, credits prior art, builds clean-room software with AI assistance, and logs decisions. The four reading routes If you are looking for a guided sequence rather than browsing the full list, use the four curated routes at the top of /guides/ : 1. New to the site: For first-time visitors wanting to understand how the tools work, where data goes, and how to verify calculations (Getting started, What happens to what you type, Check a tool’s answer, and Common questions). 2. New to government contracting: For engineers and founders preparing their first bid (Read a solicitation, Answer a solicitation, Labor rates and wrap rates, Protecting government information, and Codes, registration and small business status). 3. Running your own copy: For DevOps engineers and system administrators deploying inside corporate networks or secure labs (Host your own copy with Docker, Host on Kubernetes, Host as plain files, and Run it on a closed network). 4. Building or fixing something: For developers and technical contributors (Request a tool or add your own, Build a tool that can be listed, and Work on this site). The guide reading interface Every individual guide page provides structured navigation aids: - Header Breadcrumb: Located at the top left, linking back to /guides/ and directly to the parent section anchor (for example, Guides · L.1 Start here ). - Metadata Line: Displays the official Section L designation (such as L.1.1 ), estimated reading time based on a 220 word-per-minute standard, and regulatory currency ("Checked against its sources in November 2026"). - Sticky Desktop Table of Contents: On large screens, an "On this page" sidebar follows your scroll position on the right, listing all level-2 headings ( ) for instant jumping. - Section Sibling Navigation: Below the desktop TOC, the sidebar lists all sibling guides within the current Section L category, highlighting your active page. - Collapsible Mobile TOC: On mobile devices and small viewports, the table of contents folds into an accessible accordion labeled "On this page" located immediately above the text. - Previous and Next Navigation Cards: Large cards at the bottom of the article link sequentially to the preceding and following guides across the library. Searching and filtering guides Like the tool catalog, the guides index on /guides/ includes an instant search filter: - Enter any term (e.g. wrap rate , CUI , Docker , invoice , DFARS ). - The filter matches guide titles, summaries, section names, and second-level heading topics. - Section navigation pills ( L.1 Start here , L.2 Field guides , etc.) display live match counts and jump directly to the relevant section heading.

content: Keyboard navigation and accessibility How to navigate this site ClearedStack is built to comply with federal accessibility standards (Section 508 and WCAG 2.1 Level AA) and supports complete mouse-free operation. Global site search (⌘K or /) Pressing ⌘K (on macOS), Ctrl+K (on Windows and Linux), or / anywhere on the site opens the instant site-wide search dialog. The search engine runs 100% locally in your browser memory: - Zero latency: Queries resolve in 1 to 2 milliseconds using client-side MiniSearch indexing. - Deep heading indexing: Search indexes all 18 planned tools, 22 guides, key site pages, and over 200 individual headings with direct deep links. - Keyboard operation: Use ↓ and ↑ arrow keys to highlight results, Enter to navigate directly to the page or subsection, and Escape to close the dialog. - Strict privacy: No search queries, keystrokes, or IP addresses are transmitted to external servers or search APIs. Skip to main content Pressing Tab upon initial page load reveals a high-contrast "Skip to content" link in the top left corner. Pressing Enter bypasses the header navigation and lands keyboard focus directly on the main container, allowing immediate interaction with page content. High-contrast focus rings and logical tab order All interactive elements—links, search inputs, buttons, and summary disclosures—feature high-contrast focus rings ( focus:border-accent and focus:outline-none ). Tab order follows the visual and logical structure of the document: 1. Skip link (when focused) 2. SiteHeader branding and navigation links 3. Search inputs or section jump links 4. Main article text and internal links 5. Sticky or inline table of contents 6. Footer site map and repository links Screen reader announcements Both the Tool Catalog ( /tools/ ) and Guides Index ( /guides/ ) feature real-time search result counts marked with aria-live="polite" . When you type into a filter input, screen readers announce updated match totals (for example, "4 of 18 tools") without interrupting user keystrokes. Dark mode and system preferences The site automatically detects and honors your operating system color scheme preference ( prefers-color-scheme ). High contrast is maintained in both modes: - Light mode: Warm parchment background ( f5f4ef ) with dense charcoal ink text ( 1a1d1b ) and deep copper accent highlights. - Dark mode: Tactical black/forest background ( 0b0f0d ) with off-white typography and vibrant copper accents. - Both modes strictly avoid pure 000000 or ffffff extremes to minimize eye fatigue during extended proposal reviews. Deep linking with URL fragments Every second-level heading ( ) automatically generates an anchor ID and an interactive anchor symbol ( ) linking directly to that section. You can right-click or copy any heading link to share or bookmark an exact subsection. Similarly, all CLIN categories ( pricing , proposal , cyber , market , devsecops ) and guide sections ( start , field , host , contribute , reference ) support direct fragment URLs.

content: Navigating offline and on closed networks How to navigate this site ClearedStack is engineered from the ground up to operate reliably in air-gapped facilities, Secure Compartmented Information Facilities (SCIFs), and networks with no internet connection. Zero external assets Traditional web platforms load fonts, scripts, stylesheets, and tracking beacons from third-party content delivery networks (CDNs). ClearedStack loads nothing from external servers: - Locally bundled typography: IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono fonts are packaged directly within the application bundle via @fontsource . - Zero telemetry: No Google Analytics, no tracking scripts, no third-party tags, and no remote telemetry. - Strict Content Security Policy: Production builds enforce default-src 'self' , forbidding your browser from connecting to unauthorized external endpoints. Behavior inside a SCIF or air gap When self-hosting a copy inside a secure enclave (see Run it on a closed network): - The entire interface loads at line speed from your local web server. - The interactive catalog filters and guide search work identically to the public site because all search indexes execute locally in browser memory. - No network requests leave the client machine during tool usage or document searches. External links on closed networks The guides contain references and links to official government publications, including acquisition.gov, SAM.gov, eCFR.gov, and GitHub. When viewing ClearedStack on an air-gapped system, clicking an external link will fail or time out according to your local browser network policy. All essential regulatory summaries, formula explanations, and procedural instructions are written directly into the guides themselves so you can complete your work without external internet access.

Corrections are reviewed and merged promptly. - Send an email: If you do not use GitHub or work from an environment where code repositories are restricted, send your notes directly to contact@clearedstack.com. content: How an existing tool is observed Inspect an existing tool using public pages only, audit whether data leaves the browser, and record verifiable findings. project draft intent This guide describes intent. The observation process is not running, the ClearedStack/prior-art repository does not exist yet, and nothing has been collected. Observation is Stage 3 of the prior-art engine. Once a tool or spreadsheet is identified and assigned a record ID, an observer audits its public interface to understand what problem it solves, what data it handles, and whether it could be rebuilt as an independent, client-side tool. The observation protocol is strictly passive and public.

title: The observation checklist
subtitle: How an existing tool is observed
summary: When an observer inspects a candidate, they follow a standardized sequence of checks to collect objective evidence. 1. Check access : Determine whether the tool...
content: The observation checklist How an existing tool is observed When an observer inspects a candidate, they follow a standardized sequence of checks to collect objective evidence. 1. Check access : Determine whether the tool is freely usable on the public web or restricted behind gates. 2. Audit network traffic : Monitor the browser’s Network tab during test calculations to determine whether user inputs remain local or are transmitted to remote endpoints. 3. Run offline test : Load the page, sever network connectivity (such as by turning off Wi-Fi), and run calculations to test for server dependencies. 4. Verify citations : Extract the legal authorities or standard clauses cited by the tool and cross-reference them against official government websites. 5. Archive snapshot : Submit the public URL to a permanent web archive (such as the Wayback Machine) so the exact page observed can be reviewed at any time. 6. Grade confidence : Record every observation field alongside an explicit confidence tier (Seen, Stated, or Unknown).

title: The access boundary

summary: The strictest rule of observation is that observers never bypass access controls or create credentials. If a tool requires an account, observation stops at the ...
content: The access boundary How an existing tool is observed The strictest rule of observation is that observers never bypass access controls or create credentials. If a tool requires an account, observation stops at the public surface. If a tool requires a corporate sales demonstration, a paid license, or a personal email address to view results, the observer records the vendor’s public marketing claims and marks them as unverified. The project never initiates sales calls or accepts commercial terms of service to evaluate software.

title: What gets recorded

summary: Every observed tool is documented in a structured record with verifiable evidence: - The job : A single sentence starting with an active verb describing the cor...
content: What gets recorded How an existing tool is observed Every observed tool is documented in a structured record with verifiable evidence: - The job : A single sentence starting with an active verb describing the core task (for example, “Calculate fringe and overhead rates from cost pools”). - Inputs : The specific parameters, file formats, and data fields accepted. - Outputs : The reports, numbers, tables, or export files generated. - Login requirement : Whether the tool requires an account, offers optional login, or requires zero authentication. - Tracking profile : Third-party telemetry scripts, analytics beacons, tracking cookies, and content security policy headers seen on the page. - License or copyright : The declared intellectual property terms, such as an open-source license, public domain notice, or proprietary copyright statement. - Price model : Free public utility, freemium, paid subscription, or custom enterprise quote. - Public rule cited : The official standard, regulation, or procurement clause cited, including section numbers and official links. - Date observed : The ISO date ( YYYY-MM ) when the observation was conducted. Observations older than twelve months are marked stale and re-checked before making build decisions. - Archived snapshot link : A permanent permalink to an immutable public archive capture.

title: Layers of confidence
subtitle: How an existing tool is observed
summary: Not all information on the web is equally reliable. To ensure transparent reporting, every field in an observation record is graded using three distinct confide...
content: Layers of confidence How an existing tool is observed Not all information on the web is equally reliable. To ensure transparent reporting, every field in an observation record is graded using three distinct confidence layers: - Seen : High confidence. The observer loaded the tool, entered synthetic values, verified the offline behavior, and inspected network requests. If a tool claims to run in your browser and DevTools confirms zero outbound requests during calculation, browser confinement is marked as Seen . - Stated : Moderate confidence. The vendor’s public website states that a tool calculates specific clauses or supports particular file formats, but the feature is behind an account wall. The feature is documented as Stated by the vendor. - Unknown : Low confidence. Pricing, data retention policies, or backend architecture are not documented on public pages and would require contacting sales. These fields are marked as Unknown .

title: Re-check an observation yourself

content: Re-check an observation yourself How an existing tool is observed Every observation is published with the links and archived snapshots needed to reproduce the audit in about a minute. You do not need specialized software or programming experience to re-check our findings. If your findings disagree with a published observation—for instance, if an updated tool now sends form data to a tracking server or moved behind a paywall—please report it. Open an issue on GitHub or email contact@clearedstack.com so the record can be updated.

title: What we never do
subtitle: How an existing tool is observed
summary: Observation is strictly non-intrusive. To protect user privacy, maintain legal compliance, and ensure clean-room integrity, we never: - Access or inspect non-pu...
content: What we never do How an existing tool is observed Observation is strictly non-intrusive. To protect user privacy, maintain legal compliance, and ensure clean-room integrity, we never: - Access or inspect non-public, classified, Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), or export-controlled material. - Register user accounts, create passwords, provide company email addresses, or fill out lead capture forms. - Request sales demonstrations, start free trials, or accept commercial software evaluation agreements. - Circumvent paywalls, subscription gates, authentication forms, or IP rate limits. - Solve, click through, wait out, or bypass CAPTCHAs, Turnstiles, or anti-bot verification challenges using any manual or automated method. - Disregard robots.txt instructions or terms of service restrictions regarding crawling. - Enter real company data, actual proposal text, real overhead rates, employee names, or live contract bids into any tool. All tests use published, synthetic dummy numbers. - Decompile, reverse engineer, or copy source code, markup, CSS styles, or user interface designs from an observed tool. - Conduct security audits, penetration testing, fuzzing, or vulnerability probing against external infrastructure.

summary: Government contracting paperwork carries heavy regulatory friction. Small businesses, solo practitioners, and subcontractors frequently face complex calculation...
content: Why an engine is needed How the project chooses what to build Government contracting paperwork carries heavy regulatory friction. Small businesses, solo practitioners, and subcontractors frequently face complex calculations, formatting rules, and compliance checklists. Commercial products, spreadsheets, and agency calculators exist across the industry, but they often present significant barriers: - They require paid subscriptions that small teams cannot afford. - They gate basic calculations behind sales forms, account creation, or email collection. - They embed third-party tracking scripts that report user activity. - They send proprietary bid data or labor rates to remote servers. The prior-art engine systematically discovers these existing tools to identify what jobs need solving, document where free privacy-respecting alternatives are missing, and schedule independent clean-room implementations.

title: The ten stages
subtitle: How the project chooses what to build
summary: Work flows through ten canonical stages. The sequence is linear by default, with explicit review gates, knockout criteria, and a feedback loop for maintenance. ...
content: The ten stages How the project chooses what to build Work flows through ten canonical stages. The sequence is linear by default, with explicit review gates, knockout criteria, and a feedback loop for maintenance. 1. Discover : Find a candidate tool, spreadsheet, or portal. Candidates originate from automated web sweeps, human owner findings, or community issue submissions. See How candidates are found. 2. Record : Assign a persistent record identifier (such as PA-0001 ). Normalize the URL and identify mirrors, upstream forks, and white-label re-skins. 3. Observe : Read public pages only. Capture the discrete job, required inputs, generated outputs, access requirements, network tracking profile, license, pricing model, cited public standard, and permanent web archive snapshot. See How an existing tool is observed. 4. Screen : Test the candidate against five knockout gates. A candidate that fails any gate is screened out immediately with the reason recorded. 5. Score : Grade eligible ideas against a seven-factor rubric totaling 100 points. AI agents draft factor scores with written rationales; all scores are public. See How an idea is scored and decided. 6. Decide : The human owner makes the binding determination: Build, Link, Merge, Park, or Reject. 7. Credit : Prepare a public provenance statement naming the observed tool, what job was taken, what was done differently, and the governing regulation. See How ideas are credited. 8. Build : Write an independent client-side application in its own repository, working strictly from the official regulation and decision record. The catalog status transitions from planned to building . 9. List : Verify that the finished tool satisfies all five listing conditions. The catalog status transitions to live , and provenance appears on /tools. 10. Revisit : Conduct monthly checks. If the cited regulation changes or the observed tool alters its public terms, re-open the record to update, rebuild, or retire the tool.

title: The five knockout gates

content: The five knockout gates How the project chooses what to build During Stage 4 (Screen), every candidate must satisfy five non-negotiable criteria before receiving a score: 1. Public source : The underlying calculations, rules, or checklists exist in an officially released public statute, regulation, standard, or agency bulletin. 2. Runs in the browser : The calculation or workflow can execute completely inside a web browser without a remote server, external database, or network API. 3. Private by design : The tool operates offline, requires no user account, records no telemetry, and functions under a strict content security policy. 4. One job : The tool solves one discrete task that can be stated in a single sentence starting with an active verb. Candidates solving multiple disparate jobs are split into separate records. 5. Arithmetic, not advice : The tool computes formulas, formats data, or checks rule checklists. It never provides legal opinions, subjective assessments, or contracting officer determinations.

content: Protecting government information FCI and CUI, the security requirements that come with each, how NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC fit together, and how CUI is marked. field  A government contract usually comes with information the government expects you to protect, and with security requirements that depend on what kind of information it is. This guide sorts out the vocabulary, shows which rule applies to which information, and describes the work in the order a small company would do it. The rules below were checked in November 2026. The CMMC rollout schedule was altered in 2026, and several contract clauses are being renumbered. Treat the dates and clause numbers h

Categories are listed in the national CUI Registry | | Baseline protection | 15 basic safeguards | The 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 | Neither is classified information. Classified information has entirely separate rules, facilities and clearances, and nothing in this guide applies to it. The government is responsible for telling you what is CUI under your contract and for marking it. If a contract mentions CUI but you cannot tell what you will receive or create, ask the contracting officer in writing before you price the work. The answer changes your costs.

summary: The basic safeguarding clause lists fifteen practices. In plain terms: 1. Only authorized users, devices and processes can get in. 2. Users can do only what the...
content: The 15 basic safeguards Protecting government information The basic safeguarding clause lists fifteen practices. In plain terms: 1. Only authorized users, devices and processes can get in. 2. Users can do only what they are permitted to do. 3. Connections to outside systems are controlled. 4. Nothing sensitive is posted on public systems. 5. Every user and device is identified. 6. Identities are verified before access is granted. 7. Media holding the information is wiped or destroyed before disposal. 8. Physical access to equipment is limited. 9. Visitors are escorted and physical access is logged. 10. Traffic is monitored and controlled at the network boundary. 11. Public-facing systems sit on a separate network segment. 12. Flaws are found and fixed in good time. 13. Protection against malicious code is in place. 14. That protection is kept up to date. 15. Systems and incoming files are scanned. Most companies with ordinary good practice meet most of these. The work is in confirming each one and writing down how.

content: NIST SP 800-171 Protecting government information NIST Special Publication 800-171 is the standard for protecting CUI on a contractor’s own systems. Revision 2 has 110 requirements in 14 families: | Family | Family | | --- | --- | | Access control | Media protection | | Awareness and training | Personnel security | | Audit and accountability | Physical protection | | Configuration management | Risk assessment | | Identification and authentication | Security assessment | | Incident response | System and communications protection | | Maintenance | System and information integrity | NIST published Revision 3 in 2024, which reorganizes the requirements into 17 families. The Department of Defense has continued to assess contractors against Revision 2. Use the revision your contract and the current DoD guidance name, not simply the newest one. Two documents sit beside the requirements: - A system security plan describes the system that holds CUI, its boundary, and how each requirement is met. - A plan of action and milestones lists each requirement not yet met, what will be done about it and by when.

title: Scoring an assessment
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The Department of Defense scores an 800-171 assessment with a published method. You start at 110. For each requirement that is not fully implemented, points com...
content: Scoring an assessment Protecting government information The Department of Defense scores an 800-171 assessment with a published method. You start at 110. For each requirement that is not fully implemented, points come off: 5, 3 or 1, depending on how much the requirement matters. Because the deductions add up to more than 110, a score can be negative. Two practical points follow: - The score measures what is implemented , not what is planned. A requirement on your plan of action still loses its points until it is done. - A few requirements can earn partial credit. Most cannot. Scores from self-assessments are reported to the government in the Supplier Performance Risk System. An affirmation that goes with a score is a statement made to the government by a senior official of your company. Do not sign one you cannot support.

content: Where the CMMC rollout stands Protecting government information The program rule, 32 CFR Part 170, took effect in December 2024. The contract clause followed in November 2025, with requirements to be phased in over three years. - Phase 1 began on November 10, 2025. Solicitations can require a Level 1 or Level 2 self-assessment as a condition of award. - Later phases , which were to bring in third-party Level 2 certification from November 2026 and Level 3 after that, were put on hold by the department in mid-2026. As checked for this guide, new solicitations could require only self-assessments, and no new date had been announced. This is the part of this guide most likely to be out of date when you read it. Check the Department of Defense Chief Information Officer’s CMMC pages for the current schedule, and read the solicitation for what it actually requires.

title: Where to start
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The order matters more than the speed. 1. Find the information. List where FCI and CUI will arrive, where they will be stored and who will touch them. Email, la...
content: Where to start Protecting government information The order matters more than the speed. 1. Find the information. List where FCI and CUI will arrive, where they will be stored and who will touch them. Email, laptops, file shares, cloud services, backups, printers. 2. Shrink the boundary. The requirements apply to the systems that handle the information. Keeping CUI in one separate, well-controlled environment is far cheaper than securing a whole company to that standard. 3. Check your cloud services. A cloud service that stores CUI for a defense contract has to meet the FedRAMP Moderate baseline or its equivalent. Many ordinary commercial plans do not. 4. Assess honestly. Go through the requirements one at a time and record what is implemented, with evidence. 5. Write the system security plan as you go. 6. Put every gap on the plan of action , with an owner and a date. 7. Close the gaps , starting with the ones that carry the most points. 8. Be ready to report. Know how you would detect an incident and how you would report it within 72 hours. Reporting to the Department of Defense needs an account and a certificate that take time to obtain, so set them up before you need them. A checklist tool helps with steps 4 to 6. It does not do steps 1 to 3 for you, and it cannot tell you whether a requirement is truly met.

title: Marking CUI
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: Marking tells the next person that a document needs protection. The government-wide rules are in 32 CFR Part 2002, and the Department of Defense adds its own in...
content: Marking CUI Protecting government information Marking tells the next person that a document needs protection. The government-wide rules are in 32 CFR Part 2002, and the Department of Defense adds its own in DoD Instruction 5200.48. The banner. A document containing CUI carries the marking CUI at the top of every page. Department of Defense practice is to put it at the top and the bottom. The designation indicator. The first page or cover carries a block that says who controls the information and how it may be shared. Defense marking guidance shows it in this form: Portion marks. Individual paragraphs may be marked (CUI) or (U) . If portion marking is used at all, it has to be used throughout the document. Things to remember: - Categories come from the CUI Registry. Do not invent one. - Older markings such as “For Official Use Only” are no longer applied to new documents. A document that still carries one is not automatically CUI, and not automatically free of it. - Do not mark something CUI to be safe. Marking information that does not qualify restricts it without authority. - CUI stays CUI until the government decontrols it. - Follow your contract and the marking guide from the agency you work for. Their instructions outrank a general description like this one.

content: What this does not cover Protecting government information - Classified information. Entirely separate rules. - Export controls. Technical data controlled under the ITAR or the EAR has its own rules about who may access it, on top of anything here. - Civilian agencies. A government-wide contract rule for CUI has been proposed but was not final when this guide was checked. Civilian agency contracts may carry their own security clauses. - Your particular contract. content: Is it current? Where the rules live A source can be official and still out of date on your screen. Four checks: 1. Look for the date. The eCFR shows the date its text is current as of, at the top of each page. FAR pages show the acquisition circular and its effective date. NIST publications carry a publication date and a revision number. 2. Check for something pending. A proposed rule in the Federal Register is not yet the rule, but it tells you a change is coming. 3. Check for a deviation. Agencies can direct their contracting officers to depart from the published regulation by issuing a class deviation. Defense deviations are published with the DFARS. 4. Check your contract. The version of a clause in your contract, identified by its date, is the version that binds you, even after the regulation changes. To see what a regulation said on an earlier date, the eCFR has a point-in-time view. That is how you check a tool’s figure against the rule as it stood when the tool was written.

content: Guidance is not regulation Where the rules live Agencies publish a great deal of helpful material that is not binding: frequently asked questions, guidebooks, training slides, memos. When guidance and the regulation conflict, the regulation governs.

It can run to hundreds of pages, and most of those pages are not where the decisions are. This guide explains how the document is organized so you can find the dozen facts that tell you whether to bid, and what a winning answer has to contain.
