content: The kinds of request Read a solicitation Not everything the government posts is a solicitation, and the different kinds are answered differently. | Name | What it is | What you send back | | --- | --- | --- | | Request for information (RFI) or sources sought | Market research. The government is learning who can do the work | A short description of your capability. It is not an offer and cannot win a contract | | Draft solicitation | An early version, posted for comment | Questions and comments | | Request for quotation (RFQ) | A request for prices, common for smaller and simpler buys | A quote | | Request for proposals (RFP) | The full process for negotiated contracts, with instructions and evaluation factors | A proposal, usually in several volumes | | Invitation for bids (IFB) | Sealed bidding. The award goes on price to a responsive, responsible bidder | A bid | Federal opportunities above a set dollar value are posted on SAM.gov under Contract Opportunities. Searching and reading there is free and needs no account. Downloading some attachments does need one. An RFI is worth answering. The answers help the government decide whether a purchase can be set aside for small businesses, and how to write the requirement.

title: The lettered sections
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Many solicitations follow the uniform contract format, which divides the document into thirteen lettered sections. Even when a solicitation is laid out differen...
content: The lettered sections Read a solicitation Many solicitations follow the uniform contract format, which divides the document into thirteen lettered sections. Even when a solicitation is laid out differently, people in this field use the letters as shorthand, so they are worth learning once. | Section | Title | What you find there | | --- | --- | --- | | A | Solicitation/contract form | The cover form: solicitation number, issuing office, due date and time | | B | Supplies or services and prices/costs | The line items you will price | | C | Description/specifications/statement of work | The work | | D | Packaging and marking | How deliverables are packed and labeled | | E | Inspection and acceptance | How and where the government accepts the work | | F | Deliveries or performance | Dates, period of performance, place | | G | Contract administration data | Who administers the contract, and how to invoice | | H | Special contract requirements | Terms particular to this contract: security, key personnel, transitions | | I | Contract clauses | The standard clauses, mostly by reference | | J | List of attachments | Everything attached, by title | | K | Representations, certifications and other statements | Statements you make about your company | | L | Instructions, conditions and notices to offerors | How to prepare and submit the proposal | | M | Evaluation factors for award | How the proposal will be judged | Sections A through J become the contract. Section K is carried into it by reference. Sections L and M are about the competition, and are not part of the contract. The Federal Acquisition Regulation is being rewritten. For decades the uniform contract format has been at FAR 15.204-1, and it is still there in the codified text. The overhaul text that agencies have been working from since 2025 moves it to a different section and makes it optional. Expect to see both layouts for some time, and find the rule by its title on acquisition.gov instead of trusting a section number from memory, including the ones in this guide.

title: When the letters are missing
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Purchases of commercial products and services often use a shorter layout, built around a standard form and a set of commercial clauses. There may be no Section ...
content: When the letters are missing Read a solicitation Purchases of commercial products and services often use a shorter layout, built around a standard form and a set of commercial clauses. There may be no Section L or M by name. The same content is still there under plainer headings: - Instructions to offerors is the equivalent of Section L. - Evaluation or basis for award is the equivalent of Section M. - Statement of work , performance work statement or statement of objectives is the equivalent of Section C. - Price schedule is the equivalent of Section B. Other transaction agreements, which some defense buyers use for prototypes, are not governed by the FAR at all. Their requests follow whatever format the issuing office chooses. Read them without assumptions.

title: What to read first

content: What to read first Read a solicitation Reading from page one is the slow way. This order gets you to a bid decision fastest: 1. The cover page. Due date, time and time zone. How to submit. Who to ask. 2. Section L. What you must hand in: volumes, page limits, format, required forms. 3. Section M. What the government will score, and what matters most. 4. Section C. The work itself. Can you do it? 5. Section B. How the price is structured. 6. Section H. Anything unusual: clearances, key personnel, special security terms. 7. Sections I and K. The clauses and the statements you must make. 8. Section J attachments. Often the real detail lives here: the pricing workbook, the labor category descriptions, the data requirements.

title: The first-pass list
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Before you spend a day on a solicitation, find these facts. Most are on the cover page or in Sections L and M. - Deadlines. When questions are due. When the pro...
content: The first-pass list Read a solicitation Before you spend a day on a solicitation, find these facts. Most are on the cover page or in Sections L and M. - Deadlines. When questions are due. When the proposal is due, to the minute, and in which time zone. - How to submit. A portal, email, or something else, and any size limit on files. - Who may bid. Whether the purchase is set aside for small businesses or a specific program, and under which NAICS code and size standard. See Codes, registration and small business status. - Contract type. Fixed price, time and materials, cost reimbursement, or an ordering contract with task orders. - Length. The base period and the option periods. - Place of performance. On a government site, at your own, or remote. - Security. Whether people or facilities need a clearance, and how government information must be protected. See Protecting government information. - Basis for award. Whether the government will trade price against quality, or take the lowest-priced proposal that is technically acceptable. - Past performance. How many references, how recent and how similar. - Mandatory qualifications. Certifications, registrations or experience that are pass or fail. If you fail a pass-or-fail item, nothing else in the proposal matters.

content: Amendments and questions Read a solicitation A solicitation changes after it is posted. Each change is an amendment, and each one is part of the solicitation. - Watch for amendments. On SAM.gov you can follow an opportunity. An amendment can move the due date, change the work or replace an attachment. - Acknowledge every amendment in the way the solicitation requires. A proposal that ignores an amendment can be rejected. - Ask questions in writing, by the deadline, to the person named. Answers are normally published to every bidder, so do not put anything proprietary in a question. - Do not rely on anything said informally. Only the written solicitation and its amendments count. A good question points to a page and paragraph, quotes the text and asks one thing.

subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A proposal costs real time. Before you commit, answer these honestly: - Are we eligible, and do we pass every pass-or-fail item? - Can we do the work in Section...
content: Decide whether to bid Read a solicitation A proposal costs real time. Before you commit, answer these honestly: - Are we eligible, and do we pass every pass-or-fail item? - Can we do the work in Section C with people we have or can hire? - Do we have past performance that matches what Section M asks for? - Can we meet the security requirements by the time they apply? - Does the price structure in Section B leave room to do the work properly? - Can we produce everything Section L asks for by the due date? Deciding not to bid is a legitimate result of reading a solicitation well. When the answer is yes, the next guide covers answering every requirement.

title: The five knockout gates
subtitle: How an idea is scored and decided
summary: Before an idea receives a numerical score, it must pass five binary screening gates. If an idea fails any single gate, evaluation stops immediately. The idea is...
content: The five knockout gates How an idea is scored and decided Before an idea receives a numerical score, it must pass five binary screening gates. If an idea fails any single gate, evaluation stops immediately. The idea is screened out, and the specific failure reason is logged in the public decision record. 1. Public source. The underlying rules, formulas, thresholds, or validation tables must come from officially released public materials. Codified statutes, the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), agency supplements (such as the DFARS), and NIST Special Publications qualify. Unwritten industry folklore, private consulting methodologies, and paywalled manuals do not. 2. Runs in the browser. The tool must execute entirely on the visitor’s own computer using HTML, CSS, client-side JavaScript, or WebAssembly. Workflows that require a backend server, a central database, or remote computing APIs are screened out. 3. Private by design. The tool must work offline, require no user accounts or registration, and emit zero tracking telemetry. It must operate under a strict Content Security Policy ( connect-src 'self' ) that prevents network calls. 4. One job. The tool must perform a single, focused task that can be described in one active sentence starting with a verb (such as “Calculate a fully burdened labor rate” or “Format a small-business subcontracting report”). Sprawling all-in-one management suites fail this gate, though they may be split into separate candidate proposals. 5. Arithmetic, not advice. The tool must compute numbers, structure data, or look up citations. It must never deliver subjective legal advice, evaluate past performance, or substitute for a contracting officer’s discretion.

title: The scoring rubric
subtitle: How an idea is scored and decided
summary: Ideas that pass all five gates are evaluated across seven weighted factors. Each factor receives an integer rating from 1 to 5. The rating is multiplied by the ...
content: The scoring rubric How an idea is scored and decided Ideas that pass all five gates are evaluated across seven weighted factors. Each factor receives an integer rating from 1 to 5. The rating is multiplied by the factor’s weight, yielding a composite score from 20 to 100 points. The seven factors measure practical utility and long-term maintainability: - Need for small businesses (Weight: ×4, Max: 20 points). A rating of 1 represents a rare edge case affecting few contractors. A rating of 3 represents an occasional requirement, such as an annual reporting form. A rating of 5 represents a recurring administrative bottleneck or a calculation with severe contractual penalties if misapplied. - Gap in existing free options (Weight: ×4, Max: 20 points). A rating of 1 means high-quality, free, client-side tools already exist. A rating of 3 means an agency provides a usable form or an open-source tool exists with limited accessibility. A rating of 5 means only expensive subscription software or lead-generation forms exist. - Strength of the public source (Weight: ×3, Max: 15 points). A rating of 1 represents an informal agency slide presentation or draft discussion paper. A rating of 3 represents an agency policy memorandum or interim rule. A rating of 5 represents an enacted statute, a codified regulation in Title 48 of the CFR, or a published NIST standard. - Fits in a browser (Weight: ×3, Max: 15 points). A rating of 1 indicates large datasets exceeding browser memory limits. A rating of 3 requires a bundled lookup file under two megabytes. A rating of 5 represents lightweight, pure mathematics or text transformation with zero external dependencies. - Small enough to read (Weight: ×2, Max: 10 points). A rating of 1 indicates complex, multi-state logic. A rating of 5 indicates concise, straightforward logic readable in one sitting—typically under 300 lines of core code. - Can be checked (Weight: ×2, Max: 10 points). A rating of 1 means formulas require subjective interpretation. A rating of 5 means the government publishes worked examples or official test vectors against which outputs can be verified down to the penny. - Low upkeep of reference data (Weight: ×2, Max: 10 points). A rating of 1 requires weekly or monthly scraping of shifting government pages. A rating of 3 requires an annual update of fiscal-year rate tables. A rating of 5 represents permanent statutory arithmetic that remains valid until the regulation itself is amended.

title: Decision outcomes and overrides

summary: The composite score produces a default recommendation, which the human project owner reviews: - Build (Score ≥ 75). ClearedStack designs, builds, and maintains ...
content: Decision outcomes and overrides How an idea is scored and decided The composite score produces a default recommendation, which the human project owner reviews: - Build (Score ≥ 75). ClearedStack designs, builds, and maintains a clean-room, client-side tool in its own repository under an open-source license. - Park (Score 55 to 74). The idea is valid and passed all gates, but is deferred because of missing public data files, pending federal rulemaking, or capacity constraints. It enters the backlog with a documented blocker. - Reject (Score < 55). The candidate falls below the threshold for inclusion. The rationale and points breakdown are published in the log. Two automated override rules refine this baseline: 1. The Gap = 1 override (Link over rebuild). If an idea achieves a score of 75 or higher but scores 1 on the Gap factor, an acceptable, free, and privacy-respecting tool already exists. Rather than duplicating existing open-source work, ClearedStack routes the candidate to Link , pointing users to the existing tool in guides or catalog listings. 2. The split/merge review. If an idea scores 4 or 5 on Need but 1 or 2 on Single-Job Fit, it represents a real contractor pain point bundled inside an oversized scope. The engine flags the idea for review: the owner splits it into atomic single-job tools or merges specific functions into an existing project. 1", then: "Build", detail: "Approved for development as a new client-side tool in the catalog.", }, { when: "Score ≥ 75 but Gap = 1", then: "Link", detail: "Override: an acceptable free tool already exists, so link to it rather than rebuilding.", }, { when: "Score 55 to 74", then: "Park", detail: "Valid idea deferred due to external blockers, pending rules, or capacity.", }, { when: "Score Scores are advisory. An AI assistant may draft the initial points and rationale, but the human owner holds sole decision authority. If the owner overrides a score recommendation, the decision log explicitly records the override and the reasoning behind it.

content: What you can use in a guide Work on this site Ordinary Markdown works: headings, bold text, links, numbered and bulleted lists, code blocks and tables. - Second-level headings ( ) become the table of contents and get a link of their own. Keep them short, and do not repeat one within a guide. - Links to other pages on the site start with a slash, such as /guides/your-data/ . - Tables use pipes. Put ---: under a column to align numbers to the right. - Callouts set a short passage apart: The kind can be note , check or warning . Use them sparingly. A page with five callouts has none. Two characters need care in MDX, because it reads them as code: a left curly brace and a less-than sign. Write “less than” in words, or put the text in backticks.

content: How the guides are written Work on this site The guides are for people who are good at their own work and new to this subject. A few habits keep them readable: - Plain words. If a simpler word says the same thing, use it. - Define a term the first time it appears , and add it to the glossary. - One idea per paragraph. Short sentences. - Say what to do , then why. - Cite the rule. Name the regulation and the part, so the reader can check. - Date anything that changes. Do not print a rate or a threshold without saying when it was current, or better, tell the reader where to look it up. - Made-up examples only. No real companies, contracts or rates. Guides that describe regulations should set reviewed and end with a “Sources” section.

content: What “runs in your browser” means What happens to what you type Most web applications work in two halves. The page in front of you collects what you type and sends it to a server, the server does the work, and the answer comes back. Your information has left your computer by the time you see a result. The tools listed here have only the first half. When you open one, your browser downloads the page and its code once. After that, the arithmetic, the text parsing and the file reading are all done by that code on your machine. There is no server waiting for your input, because the project does not run one. That is also why the tools cost nothing to run and need no account. There is nothing on the other end to pay for or to sign in to.

Calculations and parsers are 100% deterministic code that you can inspect in each tool’s public repository. AI tools (Claude Code and Antigravity) are used only at development time to assist the human maintainer in drafting code, documentation, and tests. All facts and formulas are verified line by line against official public regulations by a person before release. See How AI is used to build this project.

content: This website What happens to what you type clearedstack.com is a set of plain files. It has: - no accounts and no sign-in - no cookies - no analytics or visitor counting - no fonts, scripts or images loaded from other companies’ servers The last point is enforced, not just promised. Every page carries a content security policy, which is an instruction to your browser. This site’s policy says that scripts, styles, fonts and images may load only from the site itself, that the page may connect only to the site itself, and that forms may not be submitted anywhere. If a line of code tried to send something elsewhere, your browser would refuse.

If even this is more than your situation allows, run a copy inside your own network. See Host your own copy.

content: Check it yourself What happens to what you type You can confirm that a tool keeps your input on your machine in about a minute. Use made-up numbers for the test. 1. Open the tool. 2. Open your browser’s developer tools. Press F12 on Windows or Linux, or Command-Option-I on a Mac. 3. Choose the Network tab. It lists every request the page makes. 4. Clear the list. There is a clear button at the top left of the panel. 5. Use the tool as you normally would. Type numbers, paste text, load a file. 6. Watch the list. A tool that works on your machine adds nothing to the list while you type. If a request does appear, click it and look at what was sent. A request that carries what you entered is a failure of the listing rules, and the project wants to hear about it. A second check needs no developer tools. Load the tool, then disconnect from the network: turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the cable. Keep using the tool. If it still gives answers, the work is happening on your computer.

title: What can still see your screen

content: What can still see your screen What happens to what you type Keeping data off a server does not make it invisible. Everything below runs on your side, outside any website’s control: - Browser extensions. Many extensions can read every page you open. A grammar checker, a password manager or a shopping helper may see what you type. For sensitive work, use a browser profile with no extensions or a private window with extensions turned off. - Company monitoring. A work computer may record screens, keystrokes or web traffic. That is your employer’s system and their rules apply. - Clipboard tools. If you copy a rate out of a tool, a clipboard manager or a cloud clipboard may keep it. - Screen sharing. A tool open in a shared window is visible to the meeting. - Translation and “AI assistant” features built into a browser may send page text to a service. Turn them off for the tab, or use a browser without them.

content: Saved work on a shared computer What happens to what you type A tool may let you keep your work between visits by saving it in the browser’s own storage. That storage is on your computer and is not sent anywhere. It does mean the next person to use the same browser profile can open the tool and see what you left. On a shared or borrowed computer: - use a private window, which discards its storage when you close it, or - clear the site’s data when you finish, from your browser’s privacy settings. Files you export from a tool are ordinary files. Store and send them the way you would any other document with the same contents.

content: What not to enter What happens to what you type - Classified information : never. No tool listed here is approved for it, and neither is an ordinary web browser. - Controlled unclassified information (CUI) : running in a browser does not change the rules for the computer you are sitting at. Handle CUI only on a system your contract and your company’s policy allow. If that system cannot reach the internet, host a copy of the tool on it. - Export-controlled technical data : the same reasoning applies. The tool does not send it anywhere, but your obligations attach to the machine and the people who can see it. - Proprietary rates and bid data : this is yours to decide. Nothing leaves your machine, so the question is the one above: who else can see your screen and your browser. If you are unsure whether something is safe to enter, use made-up numbers first to learn how the tool behaves.
